opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core intuition is that SAEs and transcoders are fundamentally decomposing activations. They're asking, "What directions in this activation space are active on this input?" And that's really useful, but it's a bit of an indirect way of getting at what the network is actually doing, because the computation lives in the weights. The activations are kind of the shadow of the computation, not the computation itself.

With parameter decomposition, and here I'm thinking of approaches like attribution-based parameter decomposition, and then stochastic parameter decomposition, which we worked on more recently, we're trying to decompose the weights directly into components, where each component is a piece of the network's mechanism. The idea is that on any given input, only a small number of those parameter components should be needed to explain the network's behavior. So you're looking for sparsity in which mechanisms are used, rather than sparsity in which features are active.

Why does that capture simple transformations more naturally? Take a really basic example. Suppose part of the network implements something like a rotation, or a linear map that sends one subspace to another. In activation space, that one mechanism might look like a lot of different features. Every input that passes through it lands somewhere different, so an SAE might end up tiling that space with many features, or splitting it in ways that depend on the data distribution rather than on the underlying operation. You get feature splitting, and you get a dictionary that's describing the outputs of the transformation rather than the transformation itself.

A transcoder gets closer, because it's at least trying to model the input-to-output map of a layer. But it still forces the computation through a sparse bottleneck of latent features, and it usually assumes something like "sparse latents, then a linear readout." If the real mechanism is a smooth, dense-in-activations linear map, that's an awkward fit. You end up approximating one clean operation with lots of little pieces.

With parameter decomposition, that rotation is just one component, or a small number of them. It's a low-rank chunk of the weight matrix, and it's either used or not used on a given input. The description length is tiny and it matches how the network actually implements the thing. And this also matters for mechanisms that span multiple layers, since a component can live across several weight matrices at once, so you're not forced to chop a circuit at layer boundaries the way most activation-based methods implicitly do.

There's also a nice theoretical point here. The network's function is defined by its parameters, so if you can find a decomposition of the parameters that faithfully sums back to the original weights, you have a much stronger guarantee that you've accounted for the whole mechanism. With SAEs you always have reconstruction error, the "dark matter" problem, and it's never entirely clear what's hiding in there.

Now, I want to be honest that these methods are earlier-stage. They're more expensive, there are real optimization challenges, and scaling them to big language models is ongoing work. But conceptually I think decomposing the parameters is closer to the question we actually care about, which is: what are the mechanisms, and which ones does the network use on this input?

r001.rationale: The response says an SAE may tile a rotation’s outputs with many features and a transcoder may approximate it with many pieces. It does not state that either method requires a separate input–output feature pair for every feature, including for an identity transformation.

r002.rationale: The response says a rotation could be represented by one parameter component or a small number of them, presenting that as a more natural description of a simple transformation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to see it is to ask what the object is that we're actually trying to decompose. SAEs and transcoders are fundamentally about activations. You take the activation vector at some layer, and you try to write it as a sparse combination of directions. And that works reasonably well when the thing you care about really is a representation, a feature that's sitting there in the residual stream. But a lot of what a network does isn't well described as "there's a feature here" — it's described as "this transformation gets applied to the input." The network is a function, and the parameters are where the function lives.

So take a really simple case. Suppose you've got a layer that just applies a rotation, or some low-rank linear map, to part of the input. That's about as simple a computation as a network can do. If you try to capture that with an SAE, you're basically forced to tile the input space with a huge number of directions, because a rotation doesn't have a privileged basis — every input direction gets mapped somewhere different, and the dictionary has no way to say "this is one thing" except by listing a lot of examples of it. You get feature splitting, you get this combinatorial blow-up, and the thing you end up with is a description of the inputs and outputs rather than a description of the map. A transcoder has the same problem in a slightly different form, because it's still trying to predict the output activations from a sparse set of latents, and a rotation just isn't sparse in that sense.

Whereas if you decompose the parameters directly, a rotation is one component. It's a single low-rank piece of the weight matrix that you can pull out, and it's used across every input that goes through that subspace. The sparsity is now in which mechanisms are active, not in which activation directions are active. And I think that's actually the right notion of sparsity for a lot of the computations networks do. The network doesn't necessarily use a small number of directions on a given input — it uses a small number of mechanisms, and those mechanisms can be dense in activation space.

The other thing I'd say is that this gets you much closer to something like a causal story. If I've carved the weights into pieces, I can ablate a piece, and I know exactly what I've removed from the model. With an SAE, there's always this gap: the SAE isn't the model, it's an approximation of one layer's activations, and the error term is doing some unknown amount of the work. When you decompose parameters, the pieces sum back to the actual parameters. There's no separate object standing in for the model — you've just rewritten the model as a sum of parts. So "what does this component do" has a much more direct answer: it's literally a chunk of the computation.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. Parameter decomposition is harder to make work in practice right now, and there are plenty of cases where the activation-level view is the more convenient one — if you just want to know "what is the model representing at this token," an SAE is still a very reasonable tool. But for the question of what simple operations the network is actually performing, I think decomposing the parameters is the more natural unit of analysis, because that's where the operations are.

r001.rationale: The response says an SAE may need many directions to represent a rotation and that a transcoder has a similar sparsity problem. It does not state that an identity transformation requires a separate input–output feature pair for every feature.

r002.rationale: It says that with parameter decomposition, a rotation is one component of the weight matrix, directly communicating the goal of recovering a simple transformation as a single object.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that a simple computation doesn’t necessarily look simple in activation space. Take an identity map: you put a vector in, and the network passes it through unchanged. That’s a very simple transformation. But if you’re describing it using a sparse set of activation features, you may need lots of features to represent all the different inputs that can pass through it.

An SAE is primarily trying to explain activations, and a transcoder gets closer to explaining computation by predicting outputs from inputs. But both impose a particular feature-based description. That can make a transformation that acts across a whole subspace look like lots of separate things.

With parameter decomposition, the idea is to describe the transformation itself as a component of the network’s parameters. So, potentially, you can say, ‘This component copies information,’ rather than separately describing every feature that gets copied. The hope is that this gives us a more natural unit of explanation for some computations. Whether we can actually recover those components reliably is the important empirical question.

r001.rationale: The response says feature-based methods may need many features to represent identity inputs, but does not state that they require a separate input–output feature pair for every feature.

r002.rationale: It describes representing the transformation itself as one parameter component—such as a component that copies information—instead of separately describing each copied feature.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that some computations are simple as transformations, even though they don’t look particularly simple as collections of activation features. So if you start by decomposing activations, as you do with an SAE, you might have to break a very simple operation into lots of separate pieces before you can describe it.

Take an identity transformation, for example. It’s an extremely simple rule: just pass the input through. But if you’re describing it in terms of a dictionary of features, you potentially need to say, “This feature gets copied to that feature,” for every direction that matters. A transcoder learns an input-to-output map, so it’s closer to describing the computation, but its individual components still have a particular form: detecting a direction and writing out a direction.

With parameter decomposition, the idea is to decompose the transformation itself into simpler computational components. Depending on the structure you allow those components to have, something like an identity map, a rotation, or a shared operation across many features could be represented much more compactly.

So the hope is that we can find the units in which the computation is actually simple, rather than assuming that a simple computation must be a sparse collection of feature-to-feature interactions. That’s a motivation, though, rather than a guarantee that any particular parameter decomposition will recover the right structure.

r001.rationale: The response says an identity map may require describing each direction as a feature copied to another feature, and contrasts this with a transcoder’s direction-detecting and direction-writing components.

r002.rationale: It says parameter decomposition aims to represent transformations such as identity maps or rotations compactly, but does not identify recovering the transformation as a single object as a goal.
